issues.description: The problem statement (and the example Main in the template) specify a static method named acceptSupplyDelivery(String, int, int) on SealSaloon, but the solution implementation defines a static method with a different name (receiveDelivery(String, int, int)). This is a signature/name mismatch for a core API method students are expected to implement and test against. It can confuse students (they will look for acceptSupplyDelivery) and cause inconsistencies between the provided examples (Main), the UML/spec, and the reference solution.
issues.suggested_fix: Make the method name consistent across artifacts. Either rename the solution method receiveDelivery(...) to acceptSupplyDelivery(...), or update the problem statement and template Main to use receiveDelivery(...). Ensure the static signature is public static void acceptSupplyDelivery(String name, int price, int quantity) to match the UML/spec and the example usage.

issues.description: The problem statement (and the commented usage in Main) refer to a static method named acceptSupplyDelivery(String, int, int) to handle incoming ingredient deliveries, but the solution implementation defines this functionality under the name receiveDelivery(String, int, int). Template and solution Main both call acceptSupplyDelivery in their example code, while SealSaloon.java in the solution repository provides receiveDelivery. This mismatch forces students to mentally map two different method names to the same concept (handling a supply delivery) and may cause confusion when implementing or comparing to the provided solution.
issues.suggested_fix: Unify the method name across artifacts. The simplest fix is to rename SealSaloon.receiveDelivery(...) to acceptSupplyDelivery(...) (keep it static and preserve the parameters: String name, int price, int quantity) and update any internal references. Alternatively, update the problem statement and example Main usages to call receiveDelivery instead — but prefer aligning the implementation with the problem to avoid student confusion.
